Like all species of baleen whales, the Antarctic minke whale feeds on tiny creatures known as krill by filtering water through bristlelike keratin structures called baleen plates. In this way, baleen whales can eat up to 30 percent of their total mass per day. And while no one would call the Antarctic minke whale small — it can have a mass as high as 10,000 kg — it is one of the smaller whales and is much smaller than the bowhead whale, which can weight a whopping 66,000 kg and consume as much as 19,800 kg of krill per day.

Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about krill consumption among Antarctic minke and bowhead whale?
choices: The bowhead whale is able to eat more krill per day than the Antarctic minke whale is.
Both the Antarctic minke whale and the bowhead whale can eat as much as 19,800 kg of krill per day.
The quantities of krill consumed by bowhead whale has made it difficult for Antarctic minke whales to find sufficient food.
Most baleen whales included krill in their diary, but the Antarctic minke whale is less likely than the bowhead whale to do so.
explanation: Based on the text, it can most reasonably be concluded that the bowhead whale is able to eat more krill per day than the Antarctic minke whale. This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of their sizes and feeding behaviors. The text highlights that the bowhead whale, which is significantly larger than the Antarctic minke whale (weighing up to 66,000 kg compared to 10,000 kg), can consume a much larger amount of krill per day (up to 19,800 kg). In contrast, while the Antarctic minke whale is also a baleen whale that feeds on krill through baleen plates, its smaller size limits the amount of krill it can consume in comparison to larger baleen whale species like the bowhead whale. Therefore, the bowhead whale's ability to eat more krill daily is supported by its larger size and corresponding feeding capacity.

question:
Baleen whales eat up to 30 percent of their total body mass in krill (tiny shrimplike creatures) per day. So in one day, a pygmy right whale weighing 3,500 kg could eat 1,050 kg, while a bowhead whale weighing 66,000 kg could ingest a whopping 19,800 kg. Over the last century, baleen whale populations have declined, and contrary to some scientists’ expectations, so have krill populations. Matthew S. Savoca and colleagues reserve this apparent discrepancy by pointing out that baleen whales cycle iron in the ocean, helping support phytoplankton populations, which, in turn, sustain krill populations.

Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about pygmy right and bowhead whales?
choices: As krill consumption by pygmy right whales has decreased, the krill consumption of bowhead whales has increased.
The bowhead whale is able to eat more krill per day than the pygmy right whale is.
Both pygmy right and bowhead whales can eat krill, but of the two only the pygmy right whale can also subsist on phytoplankton.
Populations of both pygmy right and bowhead whales have declined significantly over the last century due to decreasing levels of iron in the ocean.
explanation:
The correct answer is B.

Here’s the clean, text-based logic:

The passage gives explicit numerical examples:

A pygmy right whale could eat 1,050 kg of krill per day.

A bowhead whale could eat 19,800 kg of krill per day.

Since 19,800 kg is far greater than 1,050 kg, it follows directly that a bowhead whale can eat more krill per day than a pygmy right whale.

Why the others don’t work:

A: The passage says nothing about changes in krill consumption by one species relative to the other.

C: The passage does not say any whale eats phytoplankton; phytoplankton support krill, not whales.

D: Whale population decline is mentioned, but not attributed to decreasing iron levels, nor specifically to these two species. Also states "declined significantly" but no where can we infer that it was significant.

question:
With an installed capacity of 35 megawatts, the Platanares geothermal power plant in Honduras offers a dependable source of renewable energy. Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s _____ the scarcity of sites with the necessary combination of high-temperature geothermal reservoirs and fractured rock limit the widespread development of such systems.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
First, always start with the hard stops.

If we stop the sentence here, then the first and second parts can stand alone.

• Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s electricity;
• the scarcity of sites with the necessary combination of high-temperature geothermal reservoirs and fractured rock limit the widespread development of such systems.

Now, we have to deal with the "though" transition.

• What are we contrasting here? The 1st and 2nd sentence? or the 2nd and 3rd sentence?
• 1st and 2nd:

• With an installed capacity of 35 megawatts, the Platanares geothermal power plant in Honduras offers a dependable source of renewable energy.
• Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s electricity.

• 2nd and 3rd:

• Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s electricity;
• the scarcity of sites with the necessary combination of high-temperature geothermal reservoirs and fractured rock limit the widespread development of such systems.

The 1st and 2nd seem like a contrast while the 2nd and 3rd seem like supportive sentences. So the "though" needs to be placed in the 2nd sentence. B) does this.

question:
Assessing the role of forests as sinks for airborne microplastics that would otherwise continue to disperse in the atmosphere, Akane Miyazaki and her team measured concentrations of plastic particulates on leaves from konara oak trees in Japan. The team used three separate extraction methods: an ultrapure water rinse, a rinse combined with ultrasonic waves, and an alkaline solution treatment that removes epicuticular wax (a surface coating on most land plants to which particles can adhere). The concentrations of particulates recovered were 7.6 percent for water extraction, 38.4 percent for ultrasonic extraction, and 53.8 percent for alkaline extraction, leading the team to conclude that previous assessments have likely underestimated forest canopies’ capacity as sinks.

Which detail, if true, would most directly support the team’s conclusion?
choices: Most studies of microplastic accumulation on leaves have utilized extraction methods that do not have a substantial effect on epicuticular wax.
Most studies of microplastic accumulation on leaves have focused on forests with diverse tree species that exhibit varying levels of epicuticular wax.
Most studies of microplastic accumulation on leaves have found particulate concentrations that greatly exceeded 53.8 percent.
Most studies of microplastic accumulation on leaves have involved the application of alkaline treatments before water and ultrasonic treatments rather than after them.

Vehicle transmissions and many other widely used mechanical systems have moving parts that rub or slide against one another, creating friction. This friction increases energy consumption and causes wear, which decreases the stability and life span of the system. Using carbon nanotubes and oil, Jun Qu and colleagues at a US Department of Energy lab have created a coating for moving parts that reduces friction to the point where it is almost nonexistent. The new coating is suitable for common applications, unlike other approaches that require special conditions.

What does the text most strongly suggest about the coating created by Qu and colleagues?
choices: It is unlikely to reduce wear in mechanical systems that have multiple moving parts.
It is unlikely to be widely used because it can be applied only under special conditions.
It can likely be used to reduce energy consumption and wear in vehicle transmissions and other common mechanical systems.
It can likely improve the energy consumption of certain mechanical systems but not of vehicle transmissions.
explanation: Because the coating nearly eliminates friction and is suitable for common applications, it is likely to reduce both energy consumption and wear in everyday mechanical systems.

question:
Probabilistic models generate predictions based on outcomes of analogous past events, but even as these models project likely outcomes, they implicitly acknowledge that lower-frequency events may occur instead. Because they accommodate multiple potential outcomes, such models may seem incompatible with causal determinism—the view that particular outcomes are inevitable given certain preconditions. But complete foreknowledge of relevant conditions is generally unavailable, suggesting that a state of uncertainty ultimately prevails in which outcomes can be predicted but not definitively foretold.

What does the text most strongly imply about the relationship between probabilistic models and causal determinism?
choices: The predictive use of probabilistic models can be reconciled with acceptance of causal determinism because causal determinism does not necessarily entail the existence of absolute certainty.
The predictive use of probabilistic models represents a rejection of causal determinism because such models associate a single event with multiple potential outcomes.
Probabilistic models reflect the influence of causal determinism because their predictions of future outcomes are informed by concrete information about past events.
Probabilistic models can be understood as compatible with causal determinism only when their predictions of future events overwhelmingly favor one potential outcome.
explanation:
The passage says probabilistic models may seem incompatible with causal determinism, but then explains that humans usually do not have complete knowledge of all relevant conditions.

The key idea is that uncertainty in our predictions does not necessarily mean outcomes are not causally determined.

Correct Answer: A
A is correct because the text suggests probabilistic models can still fit with causal determinism. Even if an outcome is inevitable under certain conditions, we usually do not know all those conditions, so we can only predict likely outcomes instead of knowing the future with absolute certainty.

Incorrect Answers:
B — Wrong because the passage does not ultimately reject causal determinism. It says probabilistic models may seem incompatible, but then explains why the two can be reconciled.

C — Wrong because using past events to make predictions does not prove that probabilistic models are influenced by causal determinism. The main point is about uncertainty caused by incomplete knowledge.

D — Wrong because the passage does not say compatibility depends on one outcome being extremely likely. Even with multiple possible predicted outcomes, probabilistic models can still be compatible with causal determinism because humans lack complete foreknowledge.

These are the 5 logical relationships that the test makers will test you on throughout the English parts of the test. However, we will focus on these for transitions questions.

You may reference this page while doing the logical relationship questions.

The 5 logical relationships:

• Support

• Adds evidence, reasons, or examples that strengthen a claim or idea.
• Examples

• Moreover, Additionally, Furthermore

• Contrast

• Shows how two ideas are different or opposed.
• Examples

• However, Alternatively, On the other hand
• Nevertheless, Regardless, Still

• Cause and Effect

• Explains how one event or idea leads to another.
• Examples

• Thus, Therefore, Consequently
• As such

• Explanation

• Clarifies, defines, or makes an idea easier to understand.
• Examples

• In other words, That is, Specifically, For example
• Indeed (used to emphasize the previous sentence)

• Sequence

• Shows the order in which events or steps occur.
• Examples

• First, Next, Later, Suddenly, Finally

These are common SAT vocab words that will show up on the test. Review them and prepare to answer multiple choice questions regarding the word and definitions.

You may reference this page while doing the vocab questions.

Vertical gene transfer involves the transmission of genetic material from a parent to offspring; horizontal gene transfer, on the other hand, involves the exchange of genetic material between organisms not in a parent-offspring relationship. <u>While horizontal gene transfer is common among prokaryotes—single-celled organisms, such as the bacteria Brevibacillus borstelensis and Lactococcus lactis—it has rarely been observed among eukaryotes (multicellular organisms).</u> However, new studies suggest that horizontal gene transfer is more common in eukaryotes than originally thought.

Which choice best states the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It indicates a distinction between the mechanics of two kinds of biological processes.
It contrasts the frequency with which a biological phenomenon has been detected in two categories of organisms.
It explains why a common perception of a biological process is flawed.
It argues that two biological phenomena are more similar than they may initially appear to be.
explanation:
Correct answer: B — It contrasts the frequency with which a biological phenomenon has been detected in two categories of organisms.

Why:
The underlined sentence explicitly compares how often horizontal gene transfer occurs in two groups:

it is common among prokaryotes, and

it has been rarely observed among eukaryotes.

That is a direct contrast in frequency of occurrence across two categories of organisms, which is exactly what choice B states.

Why the other choices don’t work (briefly):

A focuses on mechanics (how the processes work), but the mechanics were explained earlier; the underlined sentence is about how often it happens.

C describes correcting a misconception, which happens in the following sentence (“However, new studies suggest…”), not in the underlined one.

D claims the sentence argues the phenomena are similar, but the sentence actually emphasizes a difference, not a similarity.

question:
In a study by Mika R. Moran, Daniel A. Rodriguez, and colleagues, residents of Bogotá, Colombia, and Fortaleza, Brazil, were surveyed about parks in their cities. Of the 1,121 respondents from Bogotá, 71.9% indicated that they use the city's parks, and of the 938 respondents from Fortaleza, 35.7% indicated using city parks. Given that the percentage of Bogotá respondents who reported living within a 10-minute walk of a park was much lower than that reported by Fortaleza respondents, greater proximity alone can't explain the difference in park use.

The text makes which point about the difference between the proportions of Bogotá residents and Fortaleza residents using parks?
choices: It is caused by something other than the parks' proximity to city residents.
It was calculated using sources that predate the survey.
It was much larger than the researchers conducting the study expected.
It could be due to inaccuracies in the survey results.
explanation:
Correct answer: A — It is caused by something other than the parks' proximity to city residents.

Why A is correct:
The text explicitly states that greater proximity alone can’t explain the difference in park use because Bogotá residents live closer to parks less often than Fortaleza residents, yet use parks more often. That directly implies another factor must be causing the difference.

Why the others are wrong:

B: Nothing is said about sources predating the survey.

C: The text gives no indication of researchers’ expectations.

D: The text treats the data as valid; it does not suggest inaccuracies.

In a study by Mika R. Moran, Daniel A. Rodriguez, and colleagues, residents of Caracas, Venezuela, and Fortaleza, Brazil, were surveyed about parks in their cities. Of the 1,043 respondents from Caracas, 44.7% indicated that they use the city's parks, and of the 938 respondents from Fortaleza, 35.7% indicated using city parks. <u>It may be tempting to assume the difference is due to different levels of access to parks;</u> however, given that the percentage of Caracas respondents who reported living within a 10-minute walk of a park was much lower than that reported by Fortaleza respondents, greater proximity alone can't explain the difference in park use.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
choices: It introduces a counterexample to the scenario described earlier in the text.
It provides context to help understand the scope of the researchers' survey.
It marks a shift from a discussion of the researchers' conclusion to a discussion of their methods.
It presents a potential explanation for the team's findings that the text goes on to refute.
explanation:
Correct answer: D — It presents a potential explanation for the team's findings that the text goes on to refute.

Why D is correct:
The underlined sentence introduces an idea that seems reasonable (“the difference is due to access to parks”), and the word “however” signals that this explanation is about to be rejected. The following clause then directly refutes it.

Why the others are wrong:

A: A counterexample would contradict a prior claim with evidence, not introduce a tempting but flawed explanation.

B: The sentence does not give background or scope; it proposes a hypothesis.

C: There is no shift to methods—only from possible explanation to refutation.

Psychologists Gregory Bryant, Dorsa Amir, and colleagues investigated cross-cultural perceptions of spontaneous (real) laughter and volitional (fake or forced) laughter. Study participants from 21 societies, including those in Austria and Turkey, listened to randomized recordings of 18 spontaneous laughs taken from natural conversations between pairs of women and 18 volitional laughs produced separately by 18 different women in response to an experimenter's instruction to laugh. Analysis of the participants' evaluations of the laughs prompted the team to conclude that the ability to distinguish between spontaneous and volitional laughter appears to be universal across cultures.

Which quotation from a psychologist not involved in the team's study would most directly weaken the team's conclusion?
choices: “When an individual chooses to produce volitional laughter in a natural social context, the laughter often shares certain acoustic qualities, such as pitch and fluctuation of intensity, with spontaneous laughter.”

“Although the team considered the average size of communities in each society in the study, that demographic factor was found to have no effect on listeners' identifications of laughter as spontaneous or volitional.”
“Judgments of spontaneous laughter are often associated with acoustic features such as greater intensity variability and higher pitch.”
“Recent studies in communications have shown that certain acoustic features of spontaneous laughter, such as pitch and intensity, are consistent both within and across societies.”
explanation:
Correct answer: A

Why A weakens the conclusion:
The team concludes that the ability to distinguish real from fake laughter is universal across cultures. Choice A says that volitional laughter can share key acoustic qualities with spontaneous laughter in natural contexts. If fake laughter can closely resemble real laughter, then listeners’ ability to distinguish between them may not be reliable or universal, directly undermining the conclusion.

Why the others don’t weaken:

B: Says a demographic factor had no effect—this supports the study’s robustness.

C: Describes features associated with spontaneous laughter—this aligns with the team’s findings.

D: Says features are consistent across societies—this reinforces the idea of universality.

Text 1

The island of Grande Terre split from the former supercontinent Gondwana around 80 million years ago, carrying Gondwanan species from a variety of clades with it. The island was periodically submerged until 37 million years ago, but some researchers suggest that its current biota includes species from clades predating the split that took refuge on islands near Grande Terre during submergence events and then returned.

Text 2

Thomas R. Buckley et al. found that the crown age—the age of the most recent common ancestor of all species in the clade (i.e., the clade's founder)—of Grande Terre's clade of stick insects is 41.1 million years, which is among the oldest clade crown ages of species inhabiting the island today. Nearly all of Grande Terre's living species belong to clades that originated much more recently; for example, the crown age of the island's clade of Goodeniaceae plants is 2.0 million years.

Based on the texts, the author of Text 2 would most likely agree with which statement about the "Gondwanan species" discussed in Text 1?
choices: Most of them began recolonizing Grande Terre from nearby islands around 2.0 million years ago.
Clades to which they belong originated no earlier than 41.1 million years ago.
Few, if any, of them were members of a clade that includes species currently inhabiting Grande Terre.
Although most of them have living descendants on Grande Terre, the stick insects and Goodeniaceae plants do not.
explanation:
Correct answer: C

Why C is correct:
Text 2 emphasizes that nearly all living species on Grande Terre belong to much younger clades, with only rare exceptions (e.g., stick insects at 41.1 million years). This suggests that very few, if any, present-day species belong to ancient Gondwanan clades, matching choice C.

Why the others are wrong:

A: Incorrectly ties recolonization to 2.0 million years; that number refers only to Goodeniaceae plants.

B: Overgeneralizes from the oldest clade (41.1 million years) to all Gondwanan species.

D: Flatly contradicts Text 2, which explicitly says stick insects do belong to one of the oldest clades.

question:
Saeed M.Z.A. Tarabieh conducted a study of consumer attitudes toward Jordanian food and beverage companies and found that for consumers who value environmental conservation, their likelihood of purchasing a product decreased when their perception of the product's risk of causing environmental harm increased. Subsequently, other researchers conducted a study of various demographic groups in Chile, investigating participants' intentions to purchase a new mobile phone, and found that, on average, college students had the lowest perception among all the demographic groups in the study of the environmental risks of the mobile phone. Assuming that the results of Tarabieh's study are broadly applicable, this finding suggests that ________.

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: college students might be more likely than participants in the other demographic groups to purchase the mobile phone.
college students likely prioritize other factors over a product's environmental sustainability when making purchasing decisions.
there is not a meaningful difference in the average likelihood of purchasing environmentally friendly products among the demographic groups included in the study.
the new mobile phone is less appealing to college students than other similar products on the market are.
explanation:
Correct answer: A — college students might be more likely than participants in the other demographic groups to purchase the mobile phone.

Why A is correct:
Tarabieh’s study shows a clear relationship: for people who value environmental conservation, higher perceived environmental risk → lower likelihood of purchase.
The Chile study finds that college students perceive the lowest environmental risk of the phone. If Tarabieh’s findings apply broadly, then lower perceived risk corresponds to higher likelihood of purchase, meaning college students would be more likely to buy the phone than other groups.

Why the other choices are wrong:

B: This claims something about college students’ values, but the studies only address perceived risk, not what factors students prioritize.

C: The text actually implies a difference in likelihood (via differences in perceived risk), not a lack of one.

D: This contradicts the logic of the findings; lower perceived risk would make the phone more, not less, appealing.

Key SAT logic move:
Translate the relationship → apply it to the new group → choose the option that directly follows from that relationship, without adding assumptions.

When Anglo and African Americans moved West in the nineteenth century to begin cattle ranching, they learned the trade from Spanish-speaking Mexican vaqueros (cowboys). This is why many ranching terms come from _______ English word “lasso” (a rope) comes from the Spanish word lazo, and “cinch” (a belt) comes from cincho.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

HINT

For questions that test sentence structure and boundaries, I always start with a hard stop (meaning an answer choice that ends a sentence). In this case, that means A) and D).

The poem "The Ballad of Rudolph Reed," which was published in 1960, contains three signature elements of Gwendolyn Brooks's poetic ___ compressed lines infused with bursts of vivid imagery; syncopated rhythms, largely inspired by the blues tradition; and a keen attention to everyday life in Brooks's South Side Chicago neighborhood.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

HINT

While 95% of the time, semicolons act like a period to end a sentence, 5% of the time, they show up as punctuation to separate phrases that have a comma baked into the listed phrases.

Here, the testmaker lists out 3 things after the colon:

• terse, compressed lines infused with bursts of vivid imagery
• syncopated rhythms, largely inspired by the blues tradition
• a keen attention to everyday life in Brooks's South Side Chicago neighborhood

Since list 1 and list 2 have commas in it, the semicolon should be used to separate the 3 list of phrases.

Also note the underlined part of the sentence:
"...the blues tradition<u>; and</u> a keen attention..."

See the semi colon + and? you can't start a sentence with "and" so you would have to deduce that the paragraph is trying to list items.

Watch for this as it is becoming a trending problem on the 2025-2026 tests.

Should the Czech Republic cut taxes? As of 2017, the Czech Republic’s top tax rate (46%) was lower than the highest point on the country’s Laffer curve. A theoretical relationship between tax rates and revenues, the curve can be used to determine whether tax cuts will ultimately increase a country’s tax revenue, according to some ______ 2017 data suggested that the Czech Republic was below the threshold for a tax cut.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

HINT

For questions that test sentence structure and boundaries, I always start with a hard stop (meaning an answer choice that ends a sentence). In this case, that means A) and D).

First check to see if before the hardstop, we have a complete sentence. We do here, so we proceed.

Then I simply read the rest of the sentence to see if it's a complete sentence, which means the hard stop is correct...

or

...to see if it's incomplete, where then I would determine what type of phrase I need (dependent clause, modifier, etc).

In this case, if I choose A), then I have the following left:

• 2017 data suggested that the Czech Republic was below the threshold for a tax cut.
This is a complete sentence, so the period hardstop works.

Most of the time, the hardstop is the correct answer and will save you time.
explanation: A period properly ends the clause about economists, creating two complete and correctly punctuated sentences.

question:
With an installed capacity of 35 megawatts, the Platanares geothermal power plant in Honduras offers a dependable source of renewable energy. Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s _____ the scarcity of sites with the necessary combination of high-temperature geothermal reservoirs and fractured rock limit the widespread development of such systems.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
First, always start with the hard stops.

If we stop the sentence here, then the first and second parts can stand alone.

• Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s electricity;
• the scarcity of sites with the necessary combination of high-temperature geothermal reservoirs and fractured rock limit the widespread development of such systems.

Now, we have to deal with the "though" transition.

• What are we contrasting here? The 1st and 2nd sentence? or the 2nd and 3rd sentence?
• 1st and 2nd:

• With an installed capacity of 35 megawatts, the Platanares geothermal power plant in Honduras offers a dependable source of renewable energy.
• Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s electricity.

• 2nd and 3rd:

• Power plants like Platanares supply only a small fraction of Honduras’s electricity;
• the scarcity of sites with the necessary combination of high-temperature geothermal reservoirs and fractured rock limit the widespread development of such systems.

The 1st and 2nd seem like a contrast while the 2nd and 3rd seem like supportive sentences. So the "though" needs to be placed in the 2nd sentence. B) does this.

question: What does myopic mean?

Proto-Atlantic-Congo — a protolanguage, or ancestral language of a family or descendant (daughter) language — is said to be the common ancestor of all Atlantic-Congo languages. This designation is _____ Proto-Atlantic-Congo is only postulated, its characteristics being inferred from the linguistic properties of its 1,453 daughters.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

HINT:

I call these Sentence Structure Transition questions or SST's.

First, always start with the hard stops.

• This designation is hypothetical:
• roto-Atlantic-Congo is only postulated, its characteristics being inferred from the linguistic properties of its 1,453 daughters.
• Can I separate these two sentences? Yes.

Next, acknowledge the 3 sentences in this problem:

• Proto-Atlantic-Congo is said to be the common ancestor of all Atlantic-Congo languages.
• This designation is hypothetical:
• Proto-Atlantic-Congo is only postulated, its characteristics being inferred from the linguistic properties of its 1,453 daughters.

Then, deal with the transition word. Here it's "however," which is a contrast word so I have to find the two sentences that contrast each other:

• Sentence 1 and 2 seem to be contradictory in nature
• Sentence 3 is expanding on sentence 2's assertion that the designation is hypothetical (in sentence 3, postulated means hypothesized).

Therefore, I can conclude that I need to have the word "however" in the second sentence. Only A does this.

HINT

You'll know whether a question is testing on pronouns by looking at the answer choices. Here are the steps to solving pronoun problems:

• Read the passage and determine what noun should go in the blank. You will need to infer based on the context given.

• In this problem, I ask myself "what was a popular destination within SF Intl Airport?
• "The exhibit" was the popular destination.

• Determine if the noun is singular or plural.

The average age at which people in the United States start businesses is 35. Economist Andrés Hincapié studied why young adults are relatively less likely to start businesses and whether there are ways to increase entrepreneurship in early adulthood. Hincapié found that one impediment is lack of knowledge about the practical details of how businesses are started; he further found that simply providing young adults with good informational resources on the topic significantly alleviates this problem.

Based on the text, what would Hincapié most likely say is a promising way to increase entrepreneurship in early adulthood?
choices: Creating social networks of young adults who are interested in starting a business
Providing young adults with practical information about how to start a business
Encouraging young adults to brainstorm business ideas
Giving young adults training opportunities at a variety of businesses
explanation:
The passage identifies a specific problem, young adults lack practical knowledge about starting businesses, and then gives the solution that worked: providing good informational resources.

Hincapié would likely recommend giving young adults practical business-starting information because that directly addresses the obstacle he found.

Correct Answer: B
B is correct because the text says lack of knowledge about the practical details of starting a business is an impediment, and providing informational resources significantly alleviates that problem.

Incorrect Answers:
A — Social networks might help, but the passage does not mention networking as the solution.

C — Brainstorming ideas is different from learning the practical steps of starting a business.

D — Training at businesses may be useful, but the study specifically supports providing practical information, not workplace training.

In a 2024 study, Caihong Vanderburgh and colleagues examined whether the composition of soil microbial communities could affect plants’ flavor chemistry. Whereas Jimenez-Gomez et al. (2017) showed that adding specific bacterial or fungal strains to soil can yield increased vitamin C in strawberry crops, Vanderburgh and team applied intact microbial communities gathered from ecologically distinct settings across Colorado, including areas of aspen grove and sagebrush, to mustard plants and evaluated the flavor compounds in the plants’ seeds. This ensured that the microbial conditions in their experiment would better reflect the variation and complexity of naturally occurring communities.

Based on the text, what is the most likely reason Vanderburgh and colleagues chose to avoid the method used in the strawberry study?
choices: The microbial community in the soil from the strawberry study affected plants’ nutrition, not their flavor chemistry.
The diversity of species of microorganisms in the soil from the strawberry study was already abnormally high before the researchers added further microorganisms.
The composition of microorganisms in the soil in the strawberry study may not have been representative of a naturally existing composition.
The microbial community in the soil from the strawberry study likely included similar species to those in wild soils.
explanation:
The passage contrasts two methods: one study added specific bacterial or fungal strains, while Vanderburgh used intact microbial communities from natural settings.

Vanderburgh likely avoided the earlier method because adding selected strains would not reflect the full complexity of naturally occurring soil microbial communities.

Correct Answer: C
C is correct because the text says Vanderburgh used intact microbial communities from distinct natural settings so the experiment would better reflect the “variation and complexity of naturally occurring communities.” This implies that the strawberry study’s method, adding specific strains, may have been less representative of natural microbial compositions.

Incorrect Answers:
A — The difference between nutrition and flavor chemistry is not the main reason they avoided the method. The passage emphasizes microbial community complexity, not the outcome being measured.

B — The passage does not say the strawberry study’s soil already had abnormally high microbial diversity.

D — This says the opposite of the needed idea. If the strawberry study’s soil already included similar species to wild soils, that would make it more naturally representative, not less.

Describing the adverb as “a word that distracts,” novelist Elmore Leonard is one of several authors and literary critics to recommend minimizing the use of adverbs, especially those ending in -ly (e.g., “grudgingly”), in works of fiction. To investigate the prevalence of -ly adverbs in novels, Ben Blatt used natural language processing—machine learning technology that reads and interprets text—to calculate the rates at which these words occur in both popular fiction and in novels that commonly appear on lists of notable works of English literature, such as Willa Cather’s My Ántonia. Blatt concluded that there is a positive correlation between -ly adverb avoidance and novels’ perceived literary merit.

Which finding, if true, would most clearly be an exception to the pattern Blatt identified?
choices: The novels of Virginia Woolf, one of the most celebrated writers of the twentieth century, have an average of 116 -ly adverbs per 10,000 words, while the novels of Jane Austen, one of the most celebrated writers of the nineteenth century, have an average of 128 -ly adverbs per 10,000 words.

William Faulkner’s classic novel The Sound and the Fury has the lowest -ly adverb rate among Faulkner’s novels in Blatt’s study, while F. Scott Fitzgerald’s classic novel The Great Gatsby has the lowest -ly adverb rate among Fitzgerald’s novels in Blatt’s study.

D.H. Lawrence’s acclaimed novel Women in Love and novels by several genre fiction authors that many critics regard as lacking in artistic quality have a comparable number of -ly adverbs per 10,000 words.

Whereas award-winning and best-selling novels have on average 114 and 115 -ly adverbs per 10,000 words, respectively, fan fiction novels, which are frequently authored by nonprofessional authors, have on average 154 -ly adverbs per 10,000 words.
explanation:
Logic: To be an exception, look for a highly regarded novel with many -ly adverbs or a poorly regarded novel with few -ly adverbs. That would break the positive correlation between avoiding -ly adverbs and literary merit.

A. Incorrect: It compares two acclaimed authors and doesn't contradict the overall pattern.
B. Incorrect: Both classic novels have the lowest adverb rates among their authors' works, supporting the pattern.
C. Correct: An acclaimed novel and low-quality novels having similar adverb rates contradicts the claimed correlation.
D. Incorrect: Fan fiction having more -ly adverbs than acclaimed novels supports the pattern.

In public and political discourse, the implementation of green space in urban planning is generally treated as an obvious strategy for effective local abatement of major air pollutants (such as NO₂, O₃, and particulate matter). <u>Research indicates that the role of such spaces is nuanced, however.</u> Zander S. Venter et al. analyzed data at three spatial scales (street, neighborhood, and city) from 2010 to 2019 at air-quality monitoring stations in Albania, the US state of West Virginia, and thousands of other locations. When coupled with images from aerial surveys of vegetation patterns at those locations in the same time period, the data reveal several factors mediating the relationship between vegetation and air quality.

Which finding from the study by Venter et al., if true, would most directly support the underlined claim?
choices: The association between total green space and pollutant levels is much more variable at the smallest spatial scale than at the largest, and the association is more strongly negative in areas situated in coniferous forest biomes, especially when considering particulate matter.

Regardless of total green space, locations with policies targeting the reduction of anthropogenic emissions have experienced larger improvements in air quality than locations with policies targeting the abatement of emitted pollutants have.

The effect size of total green space on ambient air quality remained consistent by location despite localized deviations from typical weather patterns, such as heat waves, that are known to cause spikes in ambient air pollution.
There is a moderately positive association between total green space and air quality across all locations, and the association persists even when the data are disaggregated by spatial scale.
explanation:
Logic: The claim says green space has a nuanced relationship with air quality, so the best evidence should show that the relationship varies depending on conditions rather than remaining constant.

A. Correct: It shows the relationship changes by spatial scale, biome, and pollutant type.
B. Incorrect: It focuses on emissions policies rather than green space.
C. Incorrect: A consistent effect suggests the relationship is simple, not nuanced.
D. Incorrect: A uniformly positive relationship also contradicts the idea of nuance.

Probabilistic models generate predictions based on outcomes of analogous past events, but even as these models project likely outcomes, they implicitly acknowledge that lower-frequency events may occur instead. Because they accommodate multiple potential outcomes, such models may seem incompatible with causal determinism—the view that particular outcomes are inevitable given certain preconditions. But complete foreknowledge of relevant conditions is generally unavailable, suggesting that a state of uncertainty ultimately prevails in which outcomes can be predicted but not definitively foretold.

What does the text most strongly imply about the relationship between probabilistic models and causal determinism?
choices: The predictive use of probabilistic models can be reconciled with acceptance of causal determinism because causal determinism does not necessarily entail the existence of absolute certainty.
The predictive use of probabilistic models represents a rejection of causal determinism because such models associate a single event with multiple potential outcomes.
Probabilistic models reflect the influence of causal determinism because their predictions of future outcomes are informed by concrete information about past events.
Probabilistic models can be understood as compatible with causal determinism only when their predictions of future events overwhelmingly favor one potential outcome.

Optimal foraging theory (OFT) holds that animals’ foraging behaviors reflect cost-benefit trade-offs that vary by species and with dynamic ecological circumstances. One such circumstance is lunar intensity, which Burt Kotler and colleagues found to be negatively associated with foraging by greater Egyptian gerbils but Eduardo Fernández-Duque and colleagues found to be positively associated with foraging by Azara’s night monkeys. This discrepancy is explicable in terms of OFT: the monkeys’ greater reliance on vision means that higher lunar intensity benefits them more than it benefits the gerbils.

Information in the text best supports which statement about OFT?
choices: It may be weakened by the finding that the costs and benefits associated with a particular ecological circumstance vary by species.
It can explain why some species act in accordance with cost-benefit trade-offs and others do not.
It can account for observations of different species responding differently to similar ecological circumstances.
It tends to allow for a better understanding of the benefits of ecological circumstances than the costs of those circumstances.

Information in the text best supports which statement about recommender systems?
choices: While recommender systems can affect consumer behavior toward suggested products, those effects are not uniform in nature and strength across product categories.

By proposing the most useful options to consumers, recommender systems boost the online visibility of utilitarian items that otherwise tend to be overlooked.

In a 2024 study, Corrine Walsh and colleagues examined whether the composition of soil microbial communities could affect plants’ flavor chemistry. Whereas Baslam et al. (2011) showed that adding specific bacterial or fungal strains to soil can yield increased flavonoid content in spinach crops, Walsh and team applied intact microbial communities gathered from ecologically distinct settings across Colorado, including areas of ponderosa pine forest and irrigated pasture, to mustard plants and evaluated the flavor compounds in the plants’ seeds. This ensured that the microbial conditions in their experiment would better reflect the variation and complexity of naturally occurring communities.

Based on the text, what is the most likely reason Walsh and colleagues chose to avoid the method used in the spinach study?
choices: The composition of microorganisms in the soil in the spinach study may not have been representative of a naturally existing composition.
The microbial community in the soil from the spinach study affected plants’ nutrition, not their flavor chemistry.
The microbial community in the soil from the spinach study likely included similar species to those in wild soils.
The diversity of species of microorganisms in the soil from the spinach study was already abnormally high before the researchers added further microorganisms.

question:
The fifteenth-century English Heege Manuscript is unusual among collections of its kind and time given its focus on fantasy tales over more acclaimed works by celebrated medieval authors like Hoccleve. But according to professor James Wade, even more unusually, the three texts in the manuscript’s first booklet were likely copied by Richard Heege from a traveling minstrel’s repertoire book. The evidence includes performative elements such as the narrator politely addressing the audience, joking about peasants and royalty, and making jokes that could be modified to refer to the town of Radford when in nearby Brackonwet to avoid giving offense.

As presented in the text, Wade would most likely agree with which statement about the first booklet of the Heege Manuscript?
choices: It was likely a copy Heege intended to give to a traveling minstrel working in the area around Radford and Brackonwet.
The texts it includes were based on stories about the area around Radford and Brackonwet, but these names were later removed.
It was copied from a text that originated from a traveling minstrel who worked in the area around Radford and Brackonwet.
It was written down by Heege from memory based on a performance by a traveling minstrel who worked in the area around Radford and Brackonwet.
explanation:
Logic: Wade believes Heege copied the booklet from a traveling minstrel's repertoire book. The local jokes suggest that minstrel worked around Radford and Brackonwet.

Correct: C. The booklet was copied from a text that originated with a traveling minstrel from that region.

Incorrect A. The passage does not say Heege intended to give the copy to a minstrel.

Incorrect B. The names were not removed; they demonstrate local adaptation.

Incorrect D. Wade says Heege copied from a repertoire book, not from memory after a performance.

question:
In the early 1970s, art historian Michael Baxandall created an approach to viewing art called the “period eye,” which explains how to look at art through the lens of its historical period. Baxandall argued that it is critical that art historians understand and communicate the original social and cultural contexts of older works of art so that it is clear what the artists intended and how the pieces would have been understood by their original viewers. <u>Since it was first introduced, Baxandall’s period eye has significantly influenced the practice of art history.</u>

Which finding about art historians, if true, would most directly support the underlined statement?
choices: Many art historians working before the 1970s produced detailed analyses of the social and cultural contexts of older artworks, though few extended that approach to artworks produced in their own lifetimes.
For some historical periods, it is difficult for art historians to reconstruct how the original viewers of artworks understood what artists’ intentions for their works were.
Art historians working today have largely rejected the idea, common among Baxandall’s predecessors, that artists’ intentions should influence how artworks are interpreted.
Numerous art historians of the late twentieth century and twenty-first century have focused their scholarship on how various artworks were interpreted at the time of their creation.
explanation:
Logic: To show that the “period eye” significantly influenced art history, the finding must show later historians adopting Baxandall’s focus on original historical interpretation.

A. Incorrect: This suggests the approach already existed before Baxandall, weakening the claim of his influence.
B. Incorrect: Difficulty reconstructing historical viewpoints does not demonstrate his influence.
C. Incorrect: Rejecting artists’ intentions conflicts with Baxandall’s approach.
D. Correct: Later historians’ focus on how works were originally interpreted shows adoption of his method.

question:
Since 2012, a consortium of research institutions has released an annual report that ranks countries by their populations’ well-being, which the authors of the report derive using data from a globally administered survey of respondents’ self-assessed levels of happiness. However, some other scholars caution that this approach reflects a tendentious understanding of the relationship between these two metrics. For example, studies have revealed a tendency among people in some non-Western countries to regard individual happiness as less important to their well-being than other ideals (e.g., a sense of harmony or balance).

Based on the text, what is a potential weakness of the annual report issued by the consortium of research institutions?
choices: It includes survey data from a wide range of Western countries but only from a narrow set of non-Western countries.
It overlooks how philosophies regarding a particular concept have evolved over time.
It may not adequately account for cultural variations in the value attached to a particular concept.
It relies on survey responses from participants who may not be representative of their countries’ cultural norms.
explanation:
Logic: The report assumes happiness measures well-being, but the passage says some cultures value harmony or balance more than happiness.

A. Incorrect: The passage never discusses which countries were surveyed.
B. Incorrect: It discusses cultural differences, not historical change.
C. Correct: The report may fail to account for cultural differences in how well-being is defined.
D. Incorrect: The criticism concerns the measure itself, not whether participants represent their countries.

question:
Readers sometimes divide the works of twentieth-century English author Evelyn Waugh into two periods: one consisting of his early satirical novels and the other consisting of his later, more serious—even ponderous—books. Critic Seamus Perry, however, challenges that strict division. Perry argues that Waugh’s writing didn’t change over time as much as some readers have suggested. For instance, Perry contends that some of Waugh’s earliest works, notably his biography of artist Dante Gabriel Rossetti, exhibit the earnest romanticism that would characterize Waugh’s later fiction.

Based on the text, which statement about Waugh’s works would Perry most likely agree with?
choices: Regardless of when they were written, Waugh’s works have important similarities that transcend their differences.
Over time, Waugh’s works became less humorous and more focused on weightier topics.
Waugh’s works can appropriately be separated into two periods by their subject matter and tone.
The earliest of Waugh’s works exhibit a satirical tone, even if that tone is more apparent in Waugh’s later works.
explanation:
Logic: Perry argues Waugh's works are more consistent across his career than critics believe, pointing to serious qualities already present in his early writing.

A. Correct: Perry believes important similarities exist across Waugh's works regardless of when they were written.
B. Incorrect: This is the view Perry rejects.
C. Incorrect: Perry specifically challenges the strict two-period division.
D. Incorrect: Perry says early works already contained later characteristics, not that later works became more satirical.

question:
In a study of perceptions of listening ability, participants explained their position on a sociopolitical issue and then received a listener’s written summary that expressed agreement or disagreement. Within selected summaries, researchers embedded markers of attentive listening (e.g., references to specific details), hypothesizing that such indications would positively influence perceptions of listening skill even in the context of disagreement. Instead, participants consistently rated listeners who expressed disagreement as less skilled, regardless of the other traits of the listeners’ summaries.

What does the text most strongly imply about how participants responded to expressions of disagreement?
choices: Although participants were critical of expressions of disagreement, they gave higher ratings to listeners whose summaries included markers of attentiveness than to listeners whose summaries did not include these markers.

Although participants maintained their positions regardless of a summary’s level of detail, they tended to regard listeners who expressed disagreement as more attentive when these listeners provided more detailed summaries.

When participants felt personally invested in the topics they discussed, they were less likely to perceive listeners who expressed disagreement as attentive, regardless of evidence to the contrary in these listeners’ summaries.
When participants encountered summaries from listeners who expressed disagreement with their views, participants tended to disregard evidence that the listeners had in fact been attentive.
explanation:
Logic: Participants rated disagreeing listeners as poor listeners even when the summaries contained clear evidence of attentive listening. This suggests disagreement caused them to ignore that evidence.

A. Incorrect: The passage says attentiveness markers did not improve ratings when listeners disagreed.
B. Incorrect: The study measured perceived listening skill, not whether participants changed their opinions.
C. Incorrect: The passage never compares participants based on how personally invested they were.
D. Correct: Participants overlooked evidence of attentiveness simply because the listener disagreed.

question:
The following text is from Mary Crow Dog’s 1990 autobiography Lakota Woman, written in collaboration with Richard Erdoes.

At the center of the old Sioux society was the tiyospaye, the extended family group, the basic hunting band, which included grandparents, uncles, aunts, in-laws, and cousins. The tiyospaye was like a warm womb cradling all within it. Kids were never alone, always fussed over by not one but several mothers, watched and taught by several fathers.

What does the text most strongly suggest about the function of the tiyospaye?
choices: It served as the central authority for governing society.
It functioned primarily as a way to organize hunting activities.
It operated as a formal network for maintaining cultural practices.
It offered care and protection to all the members it included.
explanation:
Logic: The tiyospaye is described as a nurturing extended family in which children are cared for by many adults.

A. Incorrect: Government is never discussed.
B. Incorrect: Hunting is only one aspect of the group.
C. Incorrect: Cultural preservation is not the main emphasis.
D. Correct: The passage emphasizes care, protection, and support for members.

question:
The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare’s 1598 play Henry IV, Part 1. King Henry is addressing several noblemen who are rumored to have been disloyal to him.

KING HENRY: My blood hath been too cold and temperate,
Unapt to stir these indignities,
And you have found me, for accordingly
You tread upon my patience; but be sure
I will from henceforth rather be myself,
Mighty and to be fear’d, than my [disposition],
Which hath been smooth as oil, soft as young down,
And therefore lost that title of respect
Which the proud soul ne’er pays but to the proud.

Which statement best describes how King Henry presents himself in the text?
choices: He defends his calm disposition, which he sees as fundamental to his personality, and vows to maintain his tranquil demeanor even if it causes him to lose the respect of overly proud noblemen.

He declares that he has judged the noblemen’s conduct in an impartial manner, and that despite their attempts to regain his trust through professions of submissiveness, they have irrevocably lost his respect.
He acknowledges to the noblemen that his tolerance of their conduct has undermined their respect for him, and he resolves to display his genuine nature, which is more forceful and compels deference.

He concedes that he has treated the noblemen with indifference, which in part explains why they have defied him, but he asserts that their disrespectful behavior is primarily driven by their excessive pride.
explanation:
Logic: King Henry admits his patience has made the noblemen disrespect him, and he vows to become more forceful.

A. Incorrect: He rejects, rather than defends, his previous gentleness.
B. Incorrect: He never discusses judging the noblemen impartially.
C. Correct: He acknowledges that his tolerance weakened their respect and promises to act more powerfully.
D. Incorrect: He does not primarily blame indifference for their behavior.

question:
Some food packaging contains silver nanoparticles (Ag-NPs), which can leach into waterways and soils via wastewater. In a 2015 study, Tina Ramskov and colleagues found that Ag-NPs can accumulate in the bodies of marine annelid worms (Capitella teleta). While bioaccumulation of manufactured nanoparticles may be inherently worrisome, it has been hypothesized that Ag-NP bioaccumulation in invertebrates like C. teleta could serve a valuable proxy role, obviating the need for manufacturers to conduct costly and injurious sampling of vertebrate species—such as Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar), commonly used in regulatory compliance testing—for nanoparticle bioaccumulation, as environmental protection laws currently require.

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the hypothesis presented in the text?
choices: Compared with S. salar, C. teleta can accumulate detectable Ag-NP concentrations with significantly fewer negative effects.
C. teleta has been shown to accumulate several other types of manufactured nanoparticles in addition to Ag-NPs, whereas S. salar has been shown to accumulate only Ag-NPs.
Ag-NP concentrations in C. teleta show no reliable correlation with Ag-NP concentrations in S. salar when the two species are exposed to similar levels of Ag-NPs.
Given comparable levels of exposure to Ag-NPs, C. teleta accumulates Ag-NPs at a higher rate than S. salar does but in a fixed ratio to the rate at which S. salar does.
explanation:
Logic: For C. teleta to replace salmon as a proxy, Ag-NP levels in the worms must reliably predict Ag-NP levels in salmon.

A. Incorrect: Fewer harmful effects strengthen the case for using worms.
B. Incorrect: Accumulating other nanoparticles doesn't weaken their usefulness as a proxy.
C. Correct: If worm concentrations don't correlate with salmon concentrations, the worms cannot reliably predict salmon bioaccumulation.
D. Incorrect: A fixed ratio would actually make the worms a useful proxy.

question:
Thurgood Marshall saw litigation as a means to enact social reforms and advance equal justice for US citizens. He cited the law’s “capacity to initiate change and its flexibility to accept and mold change” as vital, breaking with the historical tradition of wielding the courts primarily to clarify or modify existing laws. This vision was realized in Marshall’s successful arguing of the 1954 Brown v. Board of Education case before the US Supreme Court, as the court’s decision to overturn the long-standing “separate but equal” doctrine revolutionized how the legal system regarded civil rights.

Based on the text, how did Marshall’s Brown v. Board of Education case most likely influence the US legal system’s approach to civil rights?
choices: It led courts to focus more on clarifying existing civil rights laws than on making modifications to them.
It established that the courts could be used as a tool for significant social change.
It inadvertently resulted in the courts taking a more cautious, incremental approach to advancing subsequent civil rights cases.
It promoted the idea that legal action is the most efficient way to create social change.
explanation:
Question 10

Logic: Marshall believed courts should create social change, not just interpret laws. Brown v. Board of Education proved that courts could fundamentally reshape civil rights law.

A. Incorrect: Marshall wanted courts to make change, not merely clarify existing laws.
B. Correct: The case demonstrated that litigation could bring about major social reform.
C. Incorrect: The passage never says the decision made later courts more cautious.
D. Incorrect: The passage doesn't compare litigation with other methods of creating change.

question:
A 2025 study performed by Simon Townsend and colleagues presents evidence that bonobos, close relatives of chimpanzees, are capable of a rudimentary compositionality in communication—that is, they can organize sounds they make such that the order carries meaning in addition to the sounds themselves. After reviewing bonobo calls recorded in forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Townsend’s team claimed that bonobos sometimes paired calls in specific orders and that the contexts of such pairs indicate they were deliberate communications rather than products of chance. The team based their claim on mathematical analysis of hundreds of hours of bonobo calls along with notes of the contexts in which they occurred.

Which finding, if true, would best support the researchers’ claim?
choices: A bonobo grunt seems to function as a request for other bonobos to join in whatever activity is ongoing, since bonobos emitting a grunt did so during potentially collaborative contexts such as feeding, nesting, and grooming.
Bonobos used a single yelp or a single peep as an imperative, but a yelp appeared to be closer to a command, while a peep tended to function as a suggestion.
When bonobos paired grunts with other calls, they did not use rules of syntax as humans do to combine groups of sounds into even larger units of meaning.
While a single whistle from a bonobo was often an attempt to organize groups, a whistle preceded by a peep sound usually occurred in the presence of a charged social situation.
explanation:
Logic: The researchers claim bonobos combine calls so that the order changes the meaning. Evidence showing one call sequence has a different meaning than a single call best supports that claim.

A. Incorrect: It explains the meaning of a single grunt only.
B. Incorrect: It compares two single calls rather than combinations.
C. Incorrect: It says bonobos lack human-like syntax, which doesn't support the claim.
D. Correct: A whistle preceded by a peep having a different meaning supports meaningful call combinations.

question:
Rafael Núñez and colleagues studied how members of the Yúpno, an Indigenous group in Papua New Guinea, conceptualize time in both spoken language and gestures. The researchers recorded Yúpno speakers explaining certain temporal words and phrases, such as kalip bishap, a past-oriented expression that translates to “past times,” and coded each speaker’s manual gestures. Previous research has found a tendency in many cultures to make temporal distinctions along imagined linear axes: for instance, Spanish speakers often refer to the left/right axis to describe events in time. Some researchers believe this tendency is universal, but Núñez and colleagues claim it is not the case.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Núñez and colleagues’ claim?
choices: Some Yúpno grammatical structures used when talking about time are also used in Spanish.
Yúpno speakers typically use their left hand to make temporal gestures regardless of whether the gestures are past oriented or future oriented.
Yúpno speakers were observed making temporal gestures both indoors and outdoors, though with greater frequency when indoors.
Future-oriented gestures used by Yúpno speakers do not, on average, point in the opposite linear direction of past-oriented gestures.
explanation:
Logic: If linear left/right timelines aren't universal, Yúpno speakers should not consistently map the past and future onto opposite directions.

A. Incorrect: Shared grammar doesn't address spatial concepts of time.
B. Incorrect: Using the same hand doesn't test directional mapping.
C. Incorrect: Indoor versus outdoor gestures are irrelevant.
D. Correct: Not pointing in opposite directions directly contradicts the supposed universal pattern.

question:
A team of public transportation experts in Oceanside, California, is creating a new light rail stop for the SPRINTER system that will serve a neighborhood in which a stop does not currently exist. To decide where to place the stop, the team is using a survey from ten years ago that asked how far neighborhood residents would be willing to walk to a light rail stop. The team also looked at studies showing that people’s willingness to walk to public transit is affected by the perceived safety of the streets they are walking along. Experts hypothesize that since people have more or less willingness to walk a given distance today than residents did ten years ago, placing the new stop based only on the older survey might result in an unsuccessful transit route.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher’s claim?
choices: There has been a sharp increase in the last ten years in cyclists who use the roads in the neighborhood that the light rail stop will service.
Current users of the SPRINTER are satisfied with the number of stops along the line.
Residents of Oceanside, California, are much less likely to use public transit on rainy days than on clear days.
The enforcement of posted speed limits in the neighborhood that the light rail stop will service has increased substantially in the last ten years.
explanation:
Logic: The claim says that since people have more or less willingness to walk a given distance today than residents did ten years ago, placing the new stop based only on the older survey might result in an unsuccessful transit route.

A. Correct: More cyclists using the roads would make the pedestrians feel less safe walking to the stop, which has the potential of making the transit route unsuccessful.

B. Incorrect: Current riders' satisfaction doesn't address walking distance.

C. Incorrect: Rain affects transit use but not whether willingness to walk has changed over ten years.

D. Incorrect: Increased speed-limit enforcement makes streets seem safer, which has the potential of making the transit route successful.

question:
From petroleum refining to fuel for residential heating, hydrogen has many applications. Currently, producing hydrogen is carbon intensive, but Alexandra M. Oliveira is one of many scholars investigating the feasibility of large-scale production of hydrogen through electrolysis, a process that emits no carbon when renewable energy is used. Oliveira suggests that although some obstacles may prevent electrolytic hydrogen from dominating energy systems, there is utility in its ability to decarbonize the petroleum and heating industries, where reducing carbon emissions is especially challenging.

Which statement about the use of hydrogen in the petroleum and heating industries is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: The adoption of electrolytic hydrogen by these industries has been impeded by concerns about how carbon intensive its production is.
Development of applications for electrolytic hydrogen is less advanced in these industries than it is in most other carbon-intensive industries.
At least some of electrolytic hydrogen’s potential to lessen these industries’ carbon emissions is as yet unrealized.
The fact that large-scale electrolytic hydrogen production is not yet available has limited these industries’ interest in pursuing hydrogen-based applications.

question:
In 2009, the US state of Montana enacted rate stability regulations (RSRs), constraining insurance companies’ latitude to raise premiums (the recurring fees policyholders pay to maintain insurance policies) once policies are in effect. Although RSRs are intended to benefit consumers, Naoki Aizawa and Ami Ko note that RSRs could curtail insurers’ profits to such a degree that insurers abandon the market, thereby reducing the competitive pressure that typically restrains premium prices for newly issued policies. To determine whether this occurred in Montana, students first collect data on the number of insurers in the state for a few years leading up to and following 2009 and the premium prices for new policies offered by those insurers.

Based on the text, what would be the most reasonable next step for the students to take to accomplish their goal?
choices: Compare changes over time in the premium price data the students have collected with changes over time in premium prices for policies that were already in effect during the same period in an otherwise similar state that had not enacted RSRs.

Compare changes over time within each of the two types of data the students have collected with changes over time in analogous data for the same period from an otherwise similar state that had not enacted RSRs.

Compare changes over time within each of the two types of data the students have collected with changes over time in the same types of data from Montana for a period beginning several years after 2009.
Compare changes over time in the insurer-number data the students have collected with changes over time in insurer-number data from another state that enacted RSRs but not during the same period.

Baleen whales eat up to 30 percent of their total body mass in krill (tiny shrimplike creatures) per day. So in one day, a humpback whale weighing 30,000 kg could eat 9,000 kg, while a southern right whale weighing 80,000 kg could ingest a whopping 24,000 kg. Over the last century, baleen whale populations have declined, and contrary to some scientists’ expectations, so have krill populations. Matthew S. Savoca and colleagues resolve this apparent discrepancy by pointing out that baleen whales cycle iron in the ocean, helping support phytoplankton populations, which, in turn, sustain krill populations.

Based on the text, what is one likely effect of the change in baleen whale populations over the last century?
choices: The maximum body sizes of humpback and southern right whales have increased over the last century.
The quantity of krill needed to support a single southern right whale has increased over the last century.
The iron richness of the krill that baleen whales eat has declined over the last century.
Populations of phytoplankton that krill feed on have declined over the last century.

question:
Scientists study the abundance and the activity ratios (AR)—the relative radioactive decay rates of two isotopes—of uranium (U) isotopes in bodies of water to track sediment transport and deposition and to monitor groundwater quality. However, isotope abundance and AR are not always uniform across a single body of water, which may affect the reliability of results if sampling is not sufficiently representative. Chen Zhao et al. analyzed concentrations of the isotope U-238 and the U-234/U-238 AR at multiple depths and locations in two lakes in China, finding no significant variation in values within the same lake.

Information in the text best supports which statement about Zhao et al.’s findings?
choices: They illustrate why scientists investigating sediment transport and deposition and groundwater quality ought to evaluate how evenly U abundance and AR are distributed in the bodies of water they are examining.
They challenge the assumption that U abundance and AR sometimes vary from lake to lake, since the U-238 concentration and U-234/U-238 AR were consistent across the sampled lakes.

They indicate that researchers performing isotopic analysis in the lakes Zhao et al. studied can likely rely on localized sampling within each lake, since values from any one location or depth are representative of the entire lake.

They demonstrate that the number of samples Zhao et al. collected from the two lakes is sufficient to yield equally reliable information about sediment transport and deposition and groundwater quality in those two lakes.

question:
Baleen whales eat up to 30 percent of their total body mass in krill (tiny shrimplike creatures) per day. So in one day, a sei whale weighing 25,000 kg could eat 7,500 kg, while a northern right whale weighing 80,000 kg could ingest a whopping 24,000 kg. Over the last century, baleen whale populations have declined, and contrary to some scientists’ expectations, so have krill populations. Matthew S. Savoca and colleagues resolve this apparent discrepancy by pointing out that baleen whales cycle iron in the ocean, helping support phytoplankton populations, which, in turn, sustain krill populations.

Based on the text, what is one likely effect of the change in baleen whale populations over the last century?
choices: The quantity of krill needed to support a single northern right whale has increased over the last century.
Populations of phytoplankton that krill feed on have declined over the last century.
The iron richness of the krill that baleen whales eat has declined over the last century.
The maximum body sizes of sei and northern right whales have increased over the last century.

question:
Because humans occupy the International Space Station (ISS), it also harbors common dust-borne fungi and bacteria found on Earth. In a study of dust collected from the ISS, the growth of fungi like Penicillium chrysogenum and bacteria like Staphylococcus pettenkoferi was acceptably low under the station’s standard 25%–75% relative humidity (RH) conditions but unacceptably high at RH of 85% and above, which could feasibly happen in station areas where crew members exercise.

Which statement about microbial growth aboard the ISS is best supported by the text?
choices: The growth rates of both P. chrysogenum and S. pettenkoferi increased gradually when RH increased incrementally from 25% to 75%.
Neither P. chrysogenum nor S. pettenkoferi is likely to grow when RH is kept below 25%.
Under normal operating conditions, there should be no microbial growth in dust on board the ISS.
Undesirable microbial growth in dust likely occurs in some locations on board the ISS.

question:
The End-Ordovician mass extinction happened approximately 440 million years ago, when about 85 percent of species (including many species of bryozoans) died off. Researchers have proposed the effects of a change in sea temperature as one mechanism that may have brought on this mass extinction. But mass extinctions, while abrupt in geological terms, unfold over thousands or millions of years: it’s likely that multiple factors drove widespread species loss.

Based on the text, the author would most likely agree with which statement about the End-Ordovician mass extinction?
choices: It likely involved the extinction of more species than is typically believed.
It occurred over a long period of time and probably had multiple causes.
It was discovered only recently and is poorly understood.
It is hard to detect in Earth’s fossil or geological records.

Given the immense scope of space, the search for extraterrestrial life is almost necessarily concentrated on the exoplanets deemed to have the most plausible chance of success—typically, atmosphere-bearing terrestrial planets orbiting within a certain range of their stars (termed the habitable zone). Claiming that Earth experienced a long transition from single-lid to plate tectonics that accelerated the emergence and evolution of complex organisms, researchers Robert J. Stern and Taras V. Gerya hold that consideration of tectonics, an often overlooked factor, could help further narrow the search for advanced extraterrestrial species.

Based on the text, what do Stern and Gerya most likely believe about the development of complex life on exoplanets?
choices: It is more likely to occur if habitable zone planets with atmospheres transition from single-lid to plate tectonics late in their history than if they transition early in their history.
It is probably more dependent on the presence of plate tectonics than on orbital distance from a host star or the presence of an atmosphere.
It is more likely to occur on habitable zone planets with atmospheres and plate tectonics than on otherwise similar planets that lack plate tectonics.
It is unlikely unless the transition from single-lid to plate tectonics occurs before the acquisition of a lasting atmosphere.

question:
Quality assessments of concrete typically focus almost exclusively on compressive strength as a measure of durability, overlooking other potentially relevant factors. Lisa Ptacek et al. therefore investigated the potential of gas permeability (vulnerability to incursion by gases), which is caused in part by excessive porosity, as a durability indicator. Their measurements and observations revealed that quality of conditions during the concrete curing phase negatively correlates with gas permeability and that high gas permeability values are associated with increased deterioration as concrete surfaces age.

Information in the text best supports which statement about Ptacek et al.’s findings?
choices: They suggest that gas permeability testing presents a more reliable indication of concrete durability than compressive strength testing does.
They bolster the claim that concrete’s susceptibility to damage decreases as its gas permeability increases.
They call into question the idea that quality of curing conditions directly affects concrete gas permeability but is unrelated to compressive strength.
They indicate that evaluation of gas permeability is an appropriate addition to concrete quality assessment procedures.
